chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Logic of Mean Reversion

lessons.title: Mean Reversion vs Momentum: Two Opposing Views of How Markets Move

children.text: Show the same price chart to two traders and you can get two completely opposite trades. A stock has just broken out to a fresh 52-week high on strong volume. The first trader buys it, convinced that a stock strong enough to make new highs usually keeps making them. The second trader starts watching it for a short, checking how far it has stretched above its own recent average, convinced that a move this fast has run ahead of itself and will give some of it back. Both traders are looking at identical data. Both have a real, published body of research behind their instinct. This lesson is about naming that disagreement properly, because Chapters 2 onward assume you already know which side of it you are trading, and why.

body.text: Momentum and mean reversion are not two trading tricks. They are two opposing beliefs about how a price responds to being pushed away from where it was. Momentum says a push tends to continue, at least for a while. Mean reversion says a push tends to snap back. Both are true, just not about the same asset, the same time frame, or the same market regime, at the same time.

markDefs.definition: The tendency for information about a company's improving prospects to spread through the market slowly rather than all at once, so the price keeps drifting up as more investors catch on.

children.text: The momentum thesis holds that a stock (or an index, or a commodity) that has been rising tends to keep rising, at least for weeks to months, because information diffuses slowly. Institutions build large positions gradually rather than all at once, analysts upgrade earnings estimates one quarter at a time instead of pricing in the full improvement immediately, and retail investors chase performance after it has already shown up in the news. This is called

, the opposite of the overreaction that drives short-term mean reversion. A well known Indian illustration is the long, multi-year uptrends of quality compounders like Titan Company, Asian Paints, and Pidilite Industries through the 2000s and 2010s. Investors who bought strength and held through routine drawdowns did far better, on average, than investors who kept waiting for a "cheap" entry that a genuinely improving business never gave them.
Mean Reversion: "What Goes Up Must Come Back to Its Average"

The mean reversion thesis, covered from Lesson 1 onward, holds the opposite: that a price which has moved unusually far from its own recent average is more likely to snap back than to keep running, because the move was driven by forced flows, overreaction, or a temporary event rather than a lasting change in fundamentals. PSU banks traded in a wide, choppy range for most of 2014 to 2020, repeatedly falling on bad-loan headlines and recovering on capital infusion or recovery news, well before their post-2022 re-rating. Traders who bought the sharp dips within that range and sold the sharp rallies were trading mean reversion. Traders who bought and held through the entire range, waiting for a breakout, were effectively betting on momentum that had not arrived yet.

body.text: Notice that both strategies can look at the exact same 52-week high and disagree. This is not a flaw in one of them. It is the reason both exist as distinct, tested disciplines rather than one obvious "correct" way to trade. Chapter 8 comes back to this: the hardest part of running a reversion strategy is knowing when the market has quietly switched from a mean-reverting regime into a trending one, using the same price series that gave no warning either way.

children.text: It is worth being precise here, because a common beginner mistake is to think mean reversion means fading every strong move. It does not. A stock making a new 52-week high on genuinely improving fundamentals, rising revenue, expanding margins, new order wins, is not a reversion candidate just because it has moved a lot. A reversion trader is not interested in "it went up". A reversion trader is interested in a specific, measurable condition: the price has moved statistically far from its own mean (a large z-score, a close well outside its Bollinger Bands) without a corresponding, lasting change in the fundamentals behind it. Chapter 2 gives you the exact statistical tools to tell "moved a lot" apart from "moved unsustainably far".

body.text: A momentum strategy applied to the mean-reverting series above would generate repeated whipsaw losses, buying every small breakout only to see it fade. A mean reversion strategy applied to the trending series would generate repeated losses of its own, fading a genuine uptrend again and again while it grinds higher. Neither tool is wrong. Applying the wrong tool to the wrong kind of price series is what is wrong.

body.title: Which regime, which tool?
body.question: A stock has spent the last four months oscillating in a well-defined ₹450 to ₹520 range, repeatedly bouncing off both ends with no clear fundamental catalyst. Which approach is better suited to this price behavior?
options: Momentum, buying every new high in anticipation of a breakout
Mean reversion, buying near ₹450 and selling near ₹520 within the established range
Neither approach works on range-bound stocks
Momentum and mean reversion always give identical signals
body.explanation: A stock oscillating within a stable, well-defined range with no fundamental catalyst is a textbook mean-reverting price series. Buying near the lower boundary and selling near the upper boundary exploits exactly this behavior. Momentum strategies underperform in range-bound conditions because every breakout attempt tends to fail and reverse.

body.title: Naming the thesis
body.textWithBlank: A trader who buys a stock because it has just made a new 52-week high, expecting the strength to continue, is trading on the ___ thesis.
body.explanation: Buying strength on the expectation that a trend continues is the defining behavior of a momentum strategy, built on underreaction and the slow diffusion of information into price.

children.text: Why This Course Stays on One Side of the Fence

Momentum deserves, and rewards, its own dedicated study: relative strength ranking, breakout systems, trend filters, and the specific risk of momentum crashes when a crowded trade unwinds all at once. This course does not attempt to teach both disciplines at once, because doing so tends to produce traders who are mediocre at each rather than sharp at either. What follows from Chapter 2 onward assumes you have chosen to trade the reversion side of this fence, and it goes deep: the statistics that identify a genuine reversion candidate, the specific strategies built on those statistics, and, in Chapter 8, the discipline required to get off the fence when the regime itself has changed underneath you.

body.title: Momentum vs Mean Reversion: Core Terms

cards.definition: The thesis that a price which has moved in a direction tends to keep moving in that direction, at least for weeks to months, driven by slow diffusion of information and gradual institutional buying or selling.
The tendency for a market to price in improving or worsening fundamentals gradually rather than all at once, the behavioral driver behind momentum.
A sharp, fast reversal in a previously trending price or strategy, typically occurring when a crowded trend runs out of new buyers or sellers and unwinds abruptly.
The prevailing statistical character of a market or price series, broadly trending or broadly mean-reverting, over a given stretch of time. The same asset can shift between regimes.

points: Momentum and mean reversion are opposing beliefs about how a price responds after moving: momentum expects the move to continue, mean reversion expects it to snap back.

Momentum is driven by underreaction, information and institutional buying diffusing into price slowly. Mean reversion is driven by overreaction, forced flows and sentiment temporarily pushing price too far.
Neither strategy is universally correct. Momentum tends to work in trending regimes, mean reversion tends to work in range-bound regimes and after event-driven overreactions.
Mean reversion does not mean fading every strong move. It means acting on a specific, measurable statistical stretch away from a defined mean, not simply on the fact that a price moved a lot.

Applying momentum tools to a mean-reverting price series, or reversion tools to a trending one, produces repeated, avoidable losses. Matching the tool to the regime matters more than either tool alone.
